schools.summary: Keil traces the unexpected turn from sleeplessness to the reading of the chronicles; Ellicott states the book's theme, 'God Himself is here, though His name be absent,' and notes on Rawlinson that Persian kings were mostly unable to read.
Wesley: how vain are man's contrivances against the omnipotent God who holds kings' hearts; Clarke reports the Targum's dream and notes Persian chronicles were poetry, apt to soothe a restless mind.
Henry: as Satan moved Haman to plot Mordecai's death, God moves the king to plot his honour; 'his sleep fled away' — he who ruled 127 provinces could not command one hour's sleep.
Gill rules out anxiety, jealousy, and fear as the cause of the wakefulness, ascribing it wholly to overruling providence — a thing Jarchi called a miracle.

outliers.note: Foregrounds the Targum's tradition that the king was warned in a dream that Haman meant to slay him and seize his throne.

themes: the king who could not command sleep

schools.summary: Keil identifies the recorded plot of Bigthana and Teresh against the king (cf. Esther 2:21-23); Ellicott points back to that earlier scene where the service was first rendered.
Henry: providence directed the reader to the very place; he relays bishop Patrick's tradition of the leaves flying back, and grounds it in the God without whom not a sparrow falls.
Gill preserves the later Targum's tradition of Shimshai the scribe, unwilling to read of Mordecai, whose leaves rolled back of themselves.

Keil fixes the terms — what greatness has been shown 'for this' — with the servants' answer that nothing was done; Ellicott adds the Persian 'royal benefactors' list and the benefactor's near-legal claim to reward.
Clarke: the king plainly found nothing in the record; Wesley offers three reasons the debt went unpaid — the king's forgetfulness, the courtiers' envy, or Mordecai's being a Jew.

Henry makes the enquiry a mirror on gratitude — better honour than nothing, better late than never (Pharaoh's butler, Gen. 41:9) — yet notes how humility hinders preferment (Prov. 29:23) and good service goes unrewarded (Eccl. 9:14-16).
Gill: the king judged the deed worthy of reward but could not recall that any favour had been shown.

Keil explains 'who is in the court?' as the king seeking a minister to consult, per Persian custom, the question showing it was morning; Ellicott sets the two men in symmetry — the king pondering honour within, Haman primed to ask for a hanging without.

Wesley: Haman came early because malice would not let him sleep, waiting in the outer court since entry to the inner without license was death (Esther 4:11); Clarke fits the scene to the Targum's dream.
Henry draws the irony: Haman impatient to hang Mordecai with the gallows already built, the king as impatient to honour him, and it is fit the king should speak first.
Gill reads the king as simply in haste to confer some honour on Mordecai.
Henry finds unwitting design in 'Let him come in' — the man who hates Mordecai is summoned to devise his honour, the king ignorant of the quarrel, the two purposes wholly crossed.
Keil records the plain exchange: the attendants say Haman stands in the court, and the king commands that he come in.
Gill notes Haman waited in the outer court, none entering the inner unbidden.

themes: the enemy summoned to honour his foe

schools.summary: Keil renders 'to say within oneself' and catches the surpassing pride in Haman's self-comparison; Ellicott gives the literal 'the man in whose honour the king delighteth.'

Wesley: the king names no one for an impartial answer and knew nothing of the quarrel, while Haman thought himself meant with 'great reason,' given the king's recent favour; Clarke: the king gave him no time, posing a question that seemed to promise all his heart could wish.
Henry commends kings who delight to reward, then exposes Haman's double self-deception — too high an opinion of his own merits and of his interest with the king.
Gill: Haman was prevented from opening his errand by the king's question.

themes: what shall be done to the man

schools.summary: Keil unfolds Haman's answer to its full length — the royal apparel, the king's horse, the crown, a noble prince as attendant, the proclamation — noting he votes at once for the highest possible mark of honour.
Gill hears the whole man in his promptness: Haman answered 'at once,' forward to suggest the honours he hoped for himself.

themes: a subject arrayed as the king

schools.summary: Clarke reads the demand as pride and folly, the royal robe death for another to wear; Wesley identifies the purple robe interwoven with gold (Justin, Curtius).

Ellicott presses Haman's inordinate vanity, illustrates the request from Herodotus (Xerxes and Artabanus) and the horse from Joseph (Gen. 41:43) and Solomon (1 Kings 1:33), and reads the crown as literally set on the horse's head.
Gill: it was a capital crime among the Persians to wear the king's apparel (Trebazus, Artabanus), making Haman's proposal daring.
Henry: Haman prescribes honours too great for any subject, that he might appear in all the king's pomp, wanting only the sceptre.

debates.question: Does 'the crown royal set upon his head' mean a crown on the horse's head, or a royal crown for the honoured man?

sides.position: On the horse's head, as the Hebrew most literally reads, though no such Persian custom is attested and Mordecai is nowhere said to wear a crown
A royal crown for the man — why name the ordinary trappings of the steed?

themes: death to wear the royal robe

schools.summary: Henry hears in the proclamation the cry before Joseph, 'Bow the knee' (Gen. 41:43), and lifts it to the honour every Christian owes the saints, the excellent ones (Ps. 16:3).
Clarke cries 'Alas, poor Haman!' — the fable of the dog and the shadow fulfilled, grasping at the shadow and losing the substance.
Ellicott refers 'noble' and 'the street of the city' to their earlier uses (Esther 1:3; 4:6), the public square now the stage of Mordecai's triumph.
Gill passes briefly over the appointing of one of the king's most noble princes.

Henry pictures the thunderclap: had the king said 'Thou art the man,' Haman would have begged for Mordecai's hanging; instead he must honour his enemy — the king's heart unsearchable (Prov. 25:3) yet not unchangeable.

Clarke: 'O mortifying reverse of human fortune!' — the Targum has Haman beg to be killed rather than degraded; there is neither counsel nor wisdom against the Lord, and he who digs a pit falls into it.
Ellicott marks the pointed 'the Jew,' Mordecai's nationality preparing Esther's later petition with the king's fresh goodwill toward the proscribed race.
Gill fills in the errand from the Targum — the wardrobe robe and the chief horse, named Shiphregaz, as kings named favourite horses (Alexander's Bucephalus).

themes: do even so to Mordecai the Jew
the king's heart in God's hand

schools.summary: Keil states the mortification at its root — obliged to honour the very man he came to have executed; Ellicott calls it a grim study to analyse Haman's mingled self-reproach, hatred, and knowledge that he was ruined.

Henry weighs which put the greater force on himself, proud Haman or humble Mordecai, who valued the counterfeit respect no more than the concealed malice, yet welcomed the honour as a token of the king's favour.
Gill records the bare act, adding that the crown too was doubtless included though unnamed, since nothing was to fail of what was spoken.
Henry: Mordecai unpuffed returns to his duty, while Haman's heart breaks over a stooping that would not break a humble man's sleep.

Clarke sees Mordecai resume his humble station and Haman run home ashamed, the covered head a sign of shame and grief; Wesley: Mordecai neither overwhelmed by threats nor puffed by honour, Haman covered in shame at honouring his adversary by his own hands.

Ellicott: to the Eastern mind, used to seeing vizier and poor man change places, the resumption is unremarkable, the covered head a token of mourning; Keil grounds the gesture in Scripture (Jer. 14:4; 2 Sam. 15:30).
Gill: Mordecai returned to his post and office, not to sackcloth, judging the tide now turning in his favour.

themes: Mordecai returns to the gate unmoved
honour that does not puff up

schools.summary: Keil reports the household's omen — if Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, Haman shall surely fall — and the chamberlains' arrival; Ellicott hears the bitter turn in 'told' (cf. Esther 5:11) and contrasts Zeresh with the wives of the Marian martyrs.
Wesley names the 'wise men' as magicians called after the Persian manner; Clarke notes the Septuagint's added 'for the living God is with him,' unlikely from such heathens.

Henry calls the wife and friends miserable comforters, foretelling ruin they will not help him repent of, grounded on Mordecai's covenant seed and Haman's begun fall — the contest of Michael and the dragon (Rev. 12:7) no drawn battle.
Gill: Haman related the whole mortifying affair to his household.

outliers.note: Flags the Septuagint's addition to the warning — 'for the living God is with him' — as a sentiment scarcely to be expected from heathen lips.

themes: if Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews

schools.summary: Clarke draws the book's grand design — he who lays a snare falls into it, measure for measure (Matt. 7:2) — over the dreadful banquet Haman had no appetite for; Wesley marks him now slow to go for dejection.
Henry reads the timing as providence's hinge: the summons Haman thought would revive him only made him easier to run down, God timing the church's deliverance to manifest his glory.
Gill sets the plain timing — while they were yet talking, the chamberlains came.

themes: the snare that traps its setter
